title: OHSA — Organisational Health and Safety Compliance and Incident Process Flow
subtitle: Occupational Health and Safety Act 85 of 1993 (as amended by Act 181 of 1993 and Act 66 of 1995) and the General Administrative Regulations, 2003 (GN R.929, GG 25129), read with the other regulations in force under s.43 · As at 19 October 2026

overview.summary: This flow tells an employer, or a user of plant or machinery, what to do, by when, and who hands off to whom, from the moment something goes wrong at work until the matter closes and the lessons feed back into the risk assessment. It covers the standing duties that must be in place before anything happens, the immediate response, classification and reporting to the Department of Employment and Labour (DEL), recording and investigation, corrective action and committee review, dealing with inspectors and formal inquiries, and governance. A parallel track covers the continuous risk-management cycle that runs whether or not an incident occurs.

notes.heading: Legal status
notes.text: The OHS Act was last amended in 1996 (by the Labour Relations Act 66 of 1995, which moved appeals in s.35 to the Labour Court). The consolidation used for this flow was checked for updates on 31 October 2025 and shows no later amendment. The Occupational Health and Safety Amendment Bill was published for comment on 14 May 2021 (comments closed 31 July 2021); it proposes a management-system approach and stronger enforcement, but a search on 19 October 2026 found no Bill introduced in Parliament and no Act passed or in force. The General Administrative Regulations, 2003 (“GAR”) commenced on 25 June 2003 and repealed most of the 1996 GAR (GAR reg 13). Two regulation sets changed on 6 September 2026: the Physical Agents Regulations, 2024 (GN 5952, GG 52226, 6 March 2025) replaced the Environmental Regulations for Workplaces, 1987, and the Noise Exposure Regulations, 2024 (GN 5953) replaced the Noise-Induced Hearing Loss Regulations, 2003, each 18 months after promulgation. A notice amending the General Safety Regulations (GN 5954) took effect on 6 March 2025; leading commentators regard its wording as unclear (see section 15). The Major Hazard Installation Regulations, 2022 (GN R.2989, GG 47970) have been in force since 31 January 2023.

notes.heading: Labels used throughout
points: ACT = the OHS Act 85 of 1993; binding now.
GAR = the General Administrative Regulations, 2003; binding now. Offences listed in GAR reg 12.

REG = other regulations under s.43 (for example the General Safety Regulations “GSR”, Hazardous Chemical Agents, Physical Agents, Noise Exposure, Ergonomics, Construction, Driven Machinery, Electrical Installation and MHI Regulations); binding now. References marked “verify” must be checked against the official Gazette text.
BILL = the OHS Amendment Bill, 2021; not enacted. Build readiness; do not treat as a current legal duty.
BP = best practice or internal control; not a statutory deadline. Adopt as policy so it becomes binding internally.

notes.heading: Design principle
notes.text: The GAR clocks run from the incident, not from the day the OHS Manager hears of it, and “forthwith” means without delay. The flow therefore pushes facts upward within the shift, classifies the event on the day it happens, and sets internal targets well inside the statutory limits: telephone notice of a serious event within one hour of the OHS Manager learning of it; the written WCL notice within three working days (aligned with the COIDA report); Annexure 1 Part A within 24 hours; and investigation started within 48 hours, so that it can be carried out within the seven days GAR reg 9(2) allows. Where it is unclear whether an event is reportable, the flow reports it.

notes.heading: Nine interpretation points that shape the flow
points: Reading a 1993 Act in 2026. The Act still refers to the Department and Minister of Manpower, the industrial court, the Labour Relations Act 1956, the Workmen’s Compensation Act 1941, the attorney-general, the Minerals Act 1991, district surgeons and the BCEA 1983. Read these as references to the Department and Minister of Employment and Labour, the CCMA and Labour Court (GAR reg 6 already routes designation disputes to the CCMA), the LRA 1995, COIDA, the Director of Public Prosecutions, the Mine Health and Safety Act 29 of 1996 and the BCEA 1997 (Interpretation Act 33 of 1957 s.12(1) for re-enacted laws; other substitutions by later legislation, verify). The LA should confirm any substitution that decides a case.

Three tiers of duty, not one. Some events must be reported to DEL (s.24(1); GAR reg 8); a wider set must be recorded in Annexure 1 (all reportable incidents plus any incident that needed medical treatment other than first aid, GAR reg 9(1)); and everything recorded must be investigated within seven days (GAR reg 9(2)). Reportable incidents fall into three groups: injury or illness at the s.24(1)(a) level; a major incident (s.24(1)(b)); and a dangerous occurrence that endangered health or safety even if nobody was hurt (s.24(1)(c)). Figure 2 turns this into five tiers.

Counting days. Periods are calendar days, excluding the first and including the last, unless the last is a Sunday or public holiday (Interpretation Act s.4). The seven days in GAR reg 8(1)(a) and reg 9(2) run from the incident itself. The 14-day threshold in s.24(1)(a) is a prediction made at the time (“likely to be unable”), so re-test it as the absence develops. COIDA’s 7-day clock (s.39(1)) runs from the employer’s knowledge, so for most accidents the OHS clock is the earlier one.

Annexure 1 is a record, not a report. GAR reg 8 prescribes the forms WCL 1 or WCL 2 (the COIDA employer’s reports, now numbered W.Cl.1 and W.Cl.2) for the seven-day notice to the provincial director, and telephone, fax “or similar means” for the forthwith notice. Annexure 1 is the record the employer keeps at the workplace for at least three years and shows an inspector on request (GAR reg 9(1)). It does not need to be sent to DEL, although DEL may ask for it.

Who reports. The employer, or the user of the plant or machinery, reports (s.24(1)). For incidents to people other than employees, the user, employer or self-employed person reports with the particulars in GAR reg 8(3). Where several employers work on one site, each reports for its own employees, and the client’s mandatary agreement (s.37(2)) should say who notifies DEL and how information is shared. The definition of “employer” in s.1 excludes a labour broker as defined in the 1956 LRA, which suggests the client is the OHS employer of placed workers; treat the client as responsible for reporting incidents to TES workers on its premises and agree co-operation with the TES (verify).

What is excluded. Section 24(1)–(2) does not apply to a traffic accident on a public road, an incident in a private household (the householder reports to SAPS, which tells an inspector, s.24(3)(b), (4)) or an accident investigated under aviation law (s.24(3)). The Act does not apply on mines, which fall under the MHSA (s.1(3)(a)); the exclusion of ships in s.1(3)(b) has never been brought into force. Excluded events still trigger the s.8 duties, COIDA and internal recording.

“Reasonably practicable” and the hierarchy of controls. The general duty is to provide a safe working environment as far as is reasonably practicable (s.8(1)), judged by the severity of the risk, the state of knowledge, the availability of controls and their cost against the benefit (s.1 definition). Hazards must be eliminated or mitigated before resorting to personal protective equipment (s.8(2)(b)), and nothing the Act requires the employer to provide may be charged to employees (s.23).

No express right to refuse dangerous work. Unlike the MHSA, the OHS Act does not give employees an express right to leave or refuse dangerous work. It requires them to report unsafe situations (s.14(d)) and forbids victimisation for doing anything the Act allows or for refusing to do anything it prohibits (s.26(1)). A dismissal for a good-faith refusal to do work reasonably believed to be dangerous is likely to be found unfair (LRA s.188; CL, verify), and automatically unfair where the safety report was a protected disclosure (LRA s.187(1)(h); GBS PDA flow). Adopt a stop-work authority as policy (BP); the Bill proposes to strengthen this area (BILL, verify).

Presumed liability and the record. If an employee does or omits something that would be an offence for the employer, the employer is presumed to have done it unless it proves the employee acted without its connivance or permission, outside the scope of authority, and that it took all reasonable steps to prevent it; instructions alone are not enough (s.37(1)). Entries in the employer’s own records are admissible against it as admissions (s.39(3)), and an untrue entry is presumed to be a wilful falsification (s.39(4)). Records should state facts plainly, and the controls the flow builds in are the evidence of “reasonable steps”.

notes.heading: Roles used
notes.text: Chief Executive Officer (CEO, s.16(1)); Board or Social and Ethics / Risk Committee (BOARD); OHS Manager (OHSM, the s.16(2) assignee and process owner; the spine of this flow); Supervisor or Line Manager (SUP, the s.8(2)(i) supervisor); Health and Safety Representative (HSR, s.17); Health and Safety Committee (HSC, s.19); Incident Investigator (INV, GAR reg 9(2)); First Aider (FA); Occupational Health Practitioner (OHP); HR Manager (HR); COIDA Administrator (CA); Legal Adviser (LA); Procurement or Contract Manager (PROC); Employees (EMP); Contractors and mandataries (CON). External: DEL provincial director and inspectors (INSP); chief inspector (CI); Compensation Fund or licensee (CF); SAPS; Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP); approved inspection authority (AIA); Labour Court (LC); CCMA.

stages.title: Phase 0 — Readiness (standing obligations)
intro: Phase 0 has no case trigger. It must be complete before the first incident, because the employer’s defence under s.37(1) (reasonable steps), its ability to report on time and the HSRs’ ability to take part all depend on facts fixed in advance. Most Phase 0 duties are criminal offences if ignored (s.38(1)(a); GAR reg 12).

notes.heading: Employee side of Phase 0
notes.text: Employees owe their general duties from the first day (s.14), but an employee who has not been told the hazards, the rules and the scope of their authority cannot fairly be held to them, and the employer loses its s.37(1) defence.

notes.heading: Watch
notes.text: An HSR designated without the GAR reg 6 agreement, or a committee that has not met for more than three months, is both an offence (GAR reg 12(a); s.38(1)(a)) and the first thing an inspector checks after a serious incident.

steps.title: CEO accountability and s.16(2) assignments
steps.action: The CEO must, as far as reasonably practicable, ensure the employer’s duties are properly discharged (s.16(1)); the duty cannot be delegated away. Assign specific duties in writing to named managers (s.16(2)), with authority, resources and a reporting line back to the CEO. Re-assign immediately when a holder leaves (see GBS Off-Boarding flow). For a State department the head of department is the CEO (s.16(4)).

stages.title: Phase 1 — Incident, hazard report and immediate response
intro: Day 0 is the day of the incident, whenever the OHS Manager learns of it. Phase 1 makes the situation safe, gets help to the injured, protects the evidence and moves the facts up the line within the shift.

notes.heading: Employee obligations at this stage
notes.text: Report the incident by the end of the shift (s.14(e)); report unsafe situations (s.14(d)); follow emergency instructions (s.14(c)); do not interfere with the scene or with safety equipment (s.15; s.24(2)).

notes.heading: Hand-offs
notes.text: EMP → SUP or HSR (end of shift). SUP → OHSM (same shift). OHSM → HSR (same shift). OHSM → CA (same day). OHSM → SAPS and CEO (fatality).

notes.heading: Watch
notes.text: Cleaning up, repairing or restarting the machine before an inspector consents is the most common way an employer turns an incident into a separate offence. The only exceptions are preventing a further incident, removing the injured or dead, and rescue.

steps.title: Make safe
steps.trigger: Any incident, dangerous occurrence or imminent danger.
steps.action: Stop the task; isolate energy and substances; secure the area; prevent a second incident. Do not let anyone resume the task until it is safe.

stages.title: Phase 2 — Classify and report

stages.title: Investigation steps
intro: Every Tier 1 to Tier 4 event must be recorded in Annexure 1 and investigated within seven days of the incident, then finalised as soon as reasonably practicable (GAR reg 9(1)–(2)). intro: Every trigger feeds one intake. Phase 2 is the decision point: the tier decides who is told, by when, and how. Phases 3 and 4 run for every recordable event. Phase 5 is a branch: the inspectorate may act on any report, complaint or visit. The parallel track is not a phase: it is the continuous risk-management cycle that prevents incidents and that every investigation feeds back into.

referenceTables.title: Master flow at a glance
intro: Phase 2 asks the same questions in the same order for every event and stops at the first YES. The answer fixes the tier for the file, but the classification is re-tested whenever the facts change: an injury first logged as Tier 4 becomes Tier 2 as soon as it appears that the employee will be off for at least 14 days.

Read each phase column top to bottom to see who acts and who hands off; read each lane left to right to see one party’s whole job. The OHS Manager lane is the spine: every other lane connects to it, and the risk-management cycle runs underneath all the time.

rows: “Submit the written OHS incident report (Annexure 1)” within 7 days
COIDA flow 1.4; F05; interfaces register; case calendar; Section 15 item 12

Annexure 1 is the record kept at the workplace for at least 3 years and shown to an inspector on request (GAR reg 9(1)). The 7-day written notice to the provincial director is WCL 1 or WCL 2 (GAR reg 8(1)(a)). Keep Annexure 1 as a separate record. Status: implemented in GBS COIDA flow v1.1 (19 October 2026); F05 is now “OHS s.24 notice to the provincial director (W.Cl.2 / W.Cl.1) and internal Annexure 1 incident record (kept 3 years)”.
Immediate telephone or e-mail notice “as the W.Cl.2 directions require”
The duty to notify forthwith by telephone, fax or similar is in GAR reg 8(1)(b) itself, not only in the W.Cl.2 directions. Status: implemented in GBS COIDA flow v1.1 (19 October 2026).
OHS reportable trigger listed as death, unconsciousness, limb loss or 14 days’ absence only

Add major incidents and dangerous occurrences (s.24(1)(b)–(c)), which must be reported forthwith even if nobody is injured; add injury likely to cause a permanent physical defect. The 14-day case needs the WCL notice but not the forthwith notice. Status: implemented in GBS COIDA flow v1.1 (19 October 2026).
“Preserve the scene where an inspector will investigate”

Section 24(2) prohibits disturbing the site after a death, likely death or limb loss without an inspector’s consent, whether or not an inspector has said they will attend; the only exceptions are preventing a further incident, removing the injured or dead, and rescue. Status: implemented in GBS COIDA flow v1.1 (19 October 2026).
Root-cause investigation “BP within 30 days”, citing “GAR reg 9 (verify)”

GAR reg 9(2) requires every recorded incident to be investigated within 7 days of the incident and finalised as soon as reasonably practicable; GAR reg 9(4) requires the committee to examine it at its next meeting. Keep 30 days only as the target for finalising the report. Status: implemented in GBS COIDA flow v1.1 (19 October 2026): step 1.4 sets the 7-day investigation and 6.1 keeps 30 days as the BP finalisation target.
“OHS Act General Safety Regulation 2A (verify)” for testing

Confirmed: GSR 2A (inserted by GN R.928 of 2003) forbids permitting anyone who is or appears to be under the influence to enter or remain at work, and forbids being under the influence, possessing, using or offering alcohol or drugs at work; medicines are allowed only if their side effects create no risk. It does not prescribe any testing method: the testing procedure must come from policy.
Health records from occupational exposure “may need far longer retention under OHS regulations (verify)”

Name the regulations that apply (for example Hazardous Chemical Agents, Asbestos Abatement, Lead, Noise Exposure) and their periods in the retention schedule (Noise Exposure Regulations reg 14: 40 years for noise risk assessment, monitoring and medical surveillance records); check each against the Gazette text, because the Noise Exposure Regulations replaced the NIHL Regulations on 6 September 2026.
“OHS Act s.16(2) and ss.17–19 appointments (replace, do not leave vacant)”

s.16(2) assignments can be re-assigned by the CEO at once. HSRs are not appointed by management: a vacancy is filled under the GAR reg 6 agreement (nomination or election) and the employer then designates in writing (s.17(1); GAR reg 7). Employer nominees on the committee are designated by the employer (s.19(3)).
“Occupational health and safety duties where driving is part of the work”
Add that a traffic accident on a public road is excluded from s.24 reporting (s.24(3)(a)), but the s.8 duties, COIDA reporting and internal recording still apply.
Recruitment, Selection and Assessment flow v2.0, 5.2 (supersedes Resourcing 5.2)

Baseline medical surveillance is required by the topic regulations where an employee will be exposed (for example chemical agents, noise, asbestos, lead); medical testing is otherwise limited by EEA s.7. Name the regulation in each case.
References to the “Environmental Regulations for Workplaces” or the “Noise-Induced Hearing Loss Regulations” (where used in GBS OHS material)
Both were repealed on 6 September 2026 and replaced by the Physical Agents Regulations, 2024 and the Noise Exposure Regulations, 2024 (GG 52226, 6 March 2025).

GAR reg 1 still lists 2003 postal addresses (for example Pietersburg, Kemptonpark). Use current DEL provincial office numbers and e-mail addresses and check them quarterly. Status: implemented in GBS COIDA flow v1.1 (19 October 2026).
Immediate notice only for “death, unconsciousness, loss of a limb or part of a limb, or … a major incident”
Extend the immediate-notice trigger to injury or illness likely to cause death or a permanent physical defect, and to s.24(1)(c) dangerous occurrences (GAR reg 8(1)(b)), as in OHSA Tier 1 and Tier 3.

intro: The Act still names the Department and Minister of Manpower, the industrial court (ss.17(2), 26(1)), the LRA 1956 (definitions of “employer”, “employers’ organisation” and “trade union”), the Workmen’s Compensation Act (ss.4(1)(c), 25), the attorney-general (ss.31–32), the Minerals Act 1991 (s.1(3)(a)), the BCEA 1983 (“office”, “shop”), the South African Medical and Dental Council, the Minister of State Expenditure, district surgeons (s.39(2)), and local authorities under the Provincial Government Act 1961. The Bill proposes technical corrections but none has been enacted.

Section 17(2)–(3) still sends failed consultation on HSR arrangements to an arbitrator designated by the President of the Industrial Court, while GAR reg 6(4)–(7) sends the same dispute to the CCMA or a bargaining council. A regulation cannot amend the Act; GAR reg 6 works in practice because the industrial court no longer exists, but the conflict should be fixed.
GAR reg 6(5)–(6) allows referral to “the CCMA or Bargaining Council” but then says only the CCMA shall conciliate.
GAR reg 3 says a certificate of exemption is signed by the chief inspector, while s.40 gives the power to exempt to the Minister. That works only through a delegation under s.42(1).

GAR reg 8(1)(a) prescribes a written form (WCL 1 or 2) only for s.24(1)(a) incidents; major incidents and dangerous occurrences (s.24(1)(b)–(c)) get a forthwith notice with no written follow-up. Conversely, the forthwith notice does not cover the 14-day absence case.

GAR reg 8(1)(a) runs “within seven days of any incident”, so the OHS clock can expire before the employer knows of the incident, unlike COIDA s.39(1). Disease cases fit poorly, because a disease is not an incident on a known date.
GAR reg 8(1)(b) is reproduced in several published versions as referring to “section 24(1)(6)”; this should read s.24(1)(b).
GAR reg 8 relies on COIDA forms (“WCL 1”, “WCL 2”, “WCL 22”) whose numbering and content are controlled by the Compensation Fund and have changed since 2003, and it still refers to fax.
GAR reg 9(2) is unclear whether the incident must be investigated (completed) or merely started within seven days, and what “the contracted period in the case of contracted workers” means.

GAR reg 10(3) contains a drafting slip (“in for the inspector to subpoena”); GAR reg 12 does not state a fine amount, relying on s.43(4); and GAR reg 13 leaves regulations 7, 10, 11 and 13 of the 1996 GAR unrepealed (confirm what, if anything, still applies, verify).
Section 1(3)(b) (exclusion of ships) has never been brought into operation, so the Act arguably still applies to vessels the exclusion was meant to cover.
The Act gives no express right to refuse or leave dangerous work, unlike MHSA s.23.

The 2025 notice amending the General Safety Regulations (GN 5954) is unclear: it repeats regulation 2(1) with apparent errors and adds regulations 13H to 13J, which duplicate regulations 6, 8 and 9 of the now-repealed Environmental Regulations. Commentators recommend that DEL withdraw and re-issue it; until then, treat 13H–13J (housekeeping, flooding, fire precautions and egress) as applicable.
The consolidation used records the Act as published in “G. 14918 2 July 2993” and annotates s.26(2) as “S 25(2) inserted”; both are typographical errors in the source.
